She calls to the herbs of the world — the grasses of Ossa, of Olympus, of Pindus, of Pelion — and makes a fire under a cauldron of bronze, fills it with water and the roots she has gathered, and stirs with a dry branch of a successful olive-tree. Into the pot she throws the blood of one sacrificed old ram, the entrails of a wolf that had preyed on men, the hoof of a lion, the marrow of a stag, the shell of a tortoise, and the liver of a long-lived crow. Æson sleeps in the brew; the witch recites the charm; and he wakes twenty years younger — the daughters of Pelias, seeing the trick, set upon their own father with the same drugs, and kill him for nothing.
summary.zh: 美狄亞攜羊毛返色薩利，求其術神助她使衰老的公公埃宋重返青春：她自奧薩山、奧林波斯、皮同、珀利翁取來各種仙草，以銅釜燉水，加公羊血、食人狼之腸、獅蹄、鹿髓、龜殼、長壽烏鴉之肝，以橄欖枝攪拌；老人浴於湯中睡去，醒來年輕二十歲。佩利亞斯之女見狀，以為同法可使父返老還童，竟親手剁父煮之——卻只換得一場空。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; violence presented as historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: Medea, come home from Colchis with the fleece and the ship, stood before her father-in-law's aged face and begged the gods of her art for a thing harder than any she had yet performed: the renewal of Æson's youth. To do it, she flew first to the herbs of the world, gathering on Ossa, on Olympus, on Pindus, and on Pelion the grasses her chariot drew out by the roots, testing some with the blade, some with her nails, and some with the sinews of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then she built an altar of turf, two in the north, two in the south, one of the east, and one of the west, and called the god of her arts; and under the clear sky she dug a trench, and put into it the blood of one sacrificed old ram, and covered it over with warm ashes and the entrails of a wolf that had preyed on men, and the hoof of a lion, and the shell of a tortoise, and the marrow of a stag, and the liver of a long-lived crow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: She filled a cauldron of bronze with water, threw in the herbs she had gathered, and stirred it with a dry branch of a successful olive-tree, all the while reciting words that the poet does not repeat aloud. Then she placed the aged Æson in the brew and let him sleep; and he woke, not only rid of old age, but a young man of twenty — twenty years fewer than the day before, and as straight as a poplar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the daughters of Pelias, seeing the miracle, promised their father — by the same witch, under the same promises — that he would be made young again. So they set upon the old man with the knife, and cut him up, and boiled him: and the pot's contents boiled the man, and nothing came out of it but the ordinary steam. Medea's kin, for whom she had done all the things she had done, were undone; and Jason's own house, for all its triumph, turned, in one night, into the house of a father cooked by his daughters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Coresus and Callirhoe: The Oracle of Dodona
title.zh: 科勒索斯與卡利羅厄：多多納神諭

region.zh: 卡呂冬與多多納（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece VII.21

summary.en: Coresus, priest of Dionysus at Calydon, loved the maiden Callirhoe and she did not love him; and when all his gifts failed, he went as a suppliant to the statue of the god. Dionysus heard his priest's prayer, and the whole city became insane, as with drink, and died beside themselves. In terror, the Calydonians sent to the oracle of Dodona — the oak and the doves of Epirus — and were told that the wrath of Dionysus would not end till Coresus either sacrificed Callirhoe or some man who should volunteer to die in her place. At the altar Coresus turned the knife on himself instead of the girl; and Callirhoe, seeing him lying dead, repented, and cut her own throat at the well that has ever since been called Callirhoe.
summary.zh: 卡呂冬酒神祭司科勒索斯愛上少女卡利羅厄而遭拒；他向神像哀告，酒神遂使全城瘋狂如醉而亡。市民懼而遣使至多多納問卜——以橡樹與鴿子為靈之神諭——得知：除非科勒索斯獻祭卡利羅厄或自願代死，否則災疫不止。祭壇之上，科勒索斯反將利刃向己；卡利羅厄見其慘死，悔恨交加，自刎於井邊——該井從此以她為名。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In this part of the city there is also a temple to Dionysus under the title of Calydonian: because the statue of the god was brought from Calydon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: And when Calydon was still inhabited, among other Calydonians who were priests to the god was one Coresus, who of all men suffered most grievously from love. He was enamoured of the maiden Callirhoe, but in proportion to the greatness of his love was the dislike of the maiden to him. And as by all his wooing and promises and gifts the maiden's mind was not in the least changed, he went as a suppliant to the statue of Dionysus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the god heard the prayer of his priest, and the Calydonians forthwith became insane, as with drink, and died beside themselves. They went therefore in their consternation to consult the oracle at Dodona: for those who dwell on this mainland, as the Aetolians and their neighbours the Acarnanians and Epirotes, believe in the oracular responses they get from doves and the oak there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: And they were oracularly informed at Dodona that it was the wrath of Dionysus that had caused this trouble, which would not end till Coresus either sacrificed to Dionysus Callirhoe, or somebody who should volunteer to die instead of her. And as the maiden found no means of escape, she fled to those who had brought her up, but obtaining no aid from them, she had nothing now left but to die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: But when all the preliminary sacrificial rites that had been ordered at Dodona had taken place, and she was led to the altar as victim, then Coresus took his place as sacrificial priest, and, yielding to love and not to anger, slew himself instead of her. And when she saw Coresus lying dead, the poor girl repented, and, moved by pity and shame at his fate, cut her own throat at the well in Calydon not far from the harbour, which has ever since been called Callirhoe after her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

title.en: The Styx: The Oath-Water of the Gods
title.zh: 斯提克斯：諸神之誓水

region.zh: 冥府之河（神話地理）

texts.period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 775-806

summary.en: Styx, eldest daughter of Ocean, is honoured above all the other gods' rivers: it is by her water that the immortals swear, and the oath once sworn has an inflexible punishment — the perjurer lies breathless for a year without ambrosia and nectar, in a swoon like death, and then, for nine years more, is banished from the councils and feasts of the gods. In the tenth year he may come back to the assemblies of Olympus; and Iris, the messenger, is sent to the rock of Styx with a golden jug whenever a god is suspected of lying.
summary.zh: 斯提克斯為俄刻阿諾斯長女，其水被諸神尊為立誓之媒：誓言一經違背，罰則不可更易——偽誓者躺臥一年不飲仙食、如昏死狀；再逐出神之議事與宴會九年；至第十年方能重返奧林波斯聚會。凡神涉偽誓，宙斯即遣伊里斯攜金瓶取斯提克斯之水。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: And there dwells the goddess loathed by the deathless gods, terrible Styx, eldest daughter of back-flowing Ocean. She lives apart from the gods in her glorious house, vaulted over with great rocks and propped on silver pillars that reach to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 775-780 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Iris, the swift-footed messenger of the gods, seldom comes to her with a message over the sea's wide back; and when strife and quarrel arise among the deathless gods, or when any of them lies, then Zeus sends Iris to bring a golden jug from the far rock: the great oath of the gods, the cold water that pours from the rock beneath the broad path of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 780-785 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the water runs under the earth, along the branch of Ocean — one part is given to Styx, and nine parts flow over the earth and the sea in silver eddies; and the part that falls from the rock is a great misery to the gods. So the tenth part is the oath-water, and the ninth are the waters of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 785-795 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And whoever of the deathless gods, that have their homes on Olympus, swears a false oath and pours out the water, lies breathless for a year — no ambrosia passes his lips, no nectar; he lies speechless on a bed, wrapt in a deep swoon, and the punishment is a coma that lasts a whole year. And when the year is ended, a worse punishment follows: for nine years he is cut off from the everlasting gods, from their councils and their feasts. In the tenth year he may come again to the assemblies of the deathless gods, who dwell in the house of Olympus; and such is the oath of the great gods, sworn upon the water of Styx.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 795-806 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.
